title: DACA Renewal Delays Leave Hundreds of Thousands in Limbo Without Work or Protection
excerpt: Processing times have ballooned from 15 days to over four months under the Trump administration, costing Dreamers their jobs, income, and sense of security as lawsuits and congressional pressure mount.
body:
• USCIS processing times for DACA renewals have surged from a median of 15 days in fiscal year 2025 to over four months, leaving thousands of recipients without valid work permits.
  • Advocacy groups have sued the Trump administration in federal court demanding data on the backlog, while dozens of lawmakers are pressing DHS for answers.
  • Recipients who lapse out of status face immediate job loss, and a recent Board of Immigration Appeals ruling found DACA alone does not protect against deportation.

Across the country, recipients of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program are losing their jobs, draining their savings, and facing the prospect of deportation — not because they did anything wrong, but because the federal government is taking months longer than usual to process their renewal applications.

The delays have transformed what was once a routine two-year renewal into a months-long ordeal. USCIS data shows the median wait time for DACA renewals climbed to about 70 days between October 2025 and February 2026, up from roughly 15 days in fiscal year 2025 — a nearly fivefold increase. By late April 2026, the agency reported that the majority of renewals were taking approximately 122 days. Advocates and legal aid groups say some applicants have waited six months or longer, according to the Associated Press.

Lives Upended Overnight

The human cost is steep. In Nevada, a healthcare worker identified only as Carolyn lost her job in March after her work permit expired while her renewal sat unprocessed for months. She had been at the same clinic for six years.

https://x.com/PNS_News/status/2080368822117073318

"I kept checking every day. We had hoped that maybe I would get it in time, but I had to leave my job. Now I don't know what to do."

— Carolyn, Nevada healthcare worker and DACA recipient

In Atlanta, Elsa Sanchez, a senior customer success manager at a healthcare IT company and single mother, was placed on unpaid leave after her DACA lapsed in April. She waited more than five months before finally receiving approval in late May — but not before pulling money from her daughter's college savings to cover rent and essentials, the AP reported.

In Florida, special education worker Melani Candia missed her renewal deadline entirely due to processing backlogs. In California, immigration attorney Maria Fernanda Madrigal — herself a DACA recipient and mother of three — was let go from her firm.

Systemic Backlog or Deliberate Strategy?

The scale of the problem has drawn pointed criticism from lawmakers in both chambers. Nevada Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto accused the administration of "intentionally delaying DACA renewals so DACA recipients go unprotected," according to the Nevada Current. Colorado Sens. John Hickenlooper and Michael Bennet, along with four House members, sent a formal letter demanding DHS expedite all pending renewals and explain what changed in the processing pipeline.

USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler pushed back, telling the AP that the agency under President Trump is "more thoroughly screening and vetting all aliens, which can lengthen processing times."

Immigration attorneys have also flagged that USCIS paused processing renewals for recipients from dozens of countries the agency described in recent policy memorandums as "high-risk." The National Immigration Law Center estimated 3,000 to 4,000 people could be affected by that freeze alone.

Legal Challenges Escalate

In late June, two legal aid organizations — East Bay Sanctuary and the Immigration Institute of the Bay Area — filed a federal lawsuit in the Northern District of California demanding transparency on renewal processing data, according to EdSource and NBC News. The groups had filed information requests in May asking why applicants from October and November 2025 were still waiting; they sued after USCIS missed its June deadline to respond.

"For the years that DACA has been in place, renewals have been fairly reliable. But now we're seeing these delays cause people to fall out of status — they're losing their jobs, their ability to support their families, and their protection against deportation."

— Hillary Li, attorney, Justice Action Center

A separate Board of Immigration Appeals decision in late April determined that DACA status alone is not enough to block deportation proceedings — a ruling that further eroded recipients' sense of security. In the first 11 months of 2025, more than 250 DACA recipients were arrested and 86 deported, according to then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.

What It Means for the Diaspora

Roughly 506,000 people hold active DACA status in the United States, and 87% are in the workforce. They contribute an estimated $17 billion annually to the economy, according to congressional data. Among them are approximately 37,000 healthcare workers, nearly 6,800 educators in California alone, and thousands more in fields from technology to law enforcement.

For immigrant communities — including Indian Americans who may know DACA recipients as coworkers, neighbors, or friends — the delays underscore the broader fragility of immigration protections that lack a permanent legislative foundation. DACA was always an executive action, never a law, and 14 years later Congress still has not passed a pathway to permanent status for Dreamers.

What to Watch

The federal lawsuit in California could force USCIS to disclose processing data and potentially compel faster adjudication. Legal experts now recommend that recipients file renewals at least 150 days — five months — before expiration, up from the traditional 120-day window. The Immigrant Legal Resource Center estimates current wait times at 3.5 to 4 months and urges recipients to consult an immigration attorney before applying.

Meanwhile, the only bipartisan immigration bill in Congress, the Dignity Act, does not specifically address DACA but aims to create a legal pathway for an estimated 11 million undocumented people. Whether it gains traction in a divided Congress remains uncertain.
